title: “BECAUSE OF THE TEMPTATION TO SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DID PAUL POINT CHRISTIANS TOWARD MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: “BECAUSE OF THE TEMPTATION TO SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DID PAUL POINT CHRISTIANS TOWARD MARRIAGE?

We live in a generation that tells us to satisfy every desire. Paul wrote to a sexually broken city and said something radically different: your body belongs to Christ—and even marriage was never meant to become permission for lust.
There are Bible verses people quote because they comfort us.
Then there are Bible verses we quietly wish would stop looking at us.
First Corinthians 7:2 is one of them.
Because Paul does not speak about sexuality as though he were discussing some distant theological puzzle.
He brings the conversation painfully close.
Close to the married Christian whose eyes have begun wandering.
Close to the single believer exhausted from fighting desires nobody knows about.
Close to the husband sleeping beside his wife while secretly feeding a fantasy life on his phone.
Close to the woman carrying desires she is ashamed to admit.
Close to the believer who loves Jesus sincerely—and still wonders why following Him has not made temptation disappear.
Close to the person who fell last night, repented this morning, and is terrified that the cycle will happen again.
Paul knew Christians like that.
He wrote to Christians like that.
And underneath his words is a truth our generation desperately needs to recover:
Jesus did not save your soul while surrendering your sexuality to the world.
He wants all of you.
Your mind.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your bedroom.
Your secret history.
Your desires.
Even the parts of you nobody sees when the door closes and the screen lights up.
That is why these words matter.
Paul writes in Greek:
Dia de tas porneias hekastos tēn heautou gynaika echetō kai hekastē ton idion andra echetō.
A careful rendering is:
“But because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.”
Notice something immediately.
Paul uses the plural πορνείας — porneias.
The word belongs to the porneia family of words and refers broadly to sexual immorality—sexual activity outside the boundaries God has established.
Paul was not writing from an ivory tower.
He was writing to Corinth.
And he was writing to people whose conversion to Christ did not magically erase their sexual histories, bodily desires, cultural conditioning, temptations, or weaknesses.
Some of them had come from profoundly sexually disordered lives.

Paul had already reminded this same church that some among them had formerly been sexually immoral, adulterers, and involved in other sins—but then came one of the most beautiful reversals in the New Testament:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Read those words again if shame has been following you.
But ye are washed.
Not “you were never dirty.”
Washed.
Christianity does not require us to pretend the stain never existed.
Christianity announces that there is a Savior powerful enough to cleanse it.
That changes how we must read 1 Corinthians 7.
Paul is not writing to pristine people who have never struggled sexually.
He is writing to redeemed sinners learning what it means for Jesus Christ to become Lord even over their bodies.
And that makes his answer astonishing.
Because Paul does not say:
“Your desires are your identity.”
He does not say:
“If you feel it strongly enough, it must be right.”
He does not say:
“Suppress everything physical because the body is evil.”
And he certainly does not say:
“Just get married and then lust becomes holy.”
Instead, Paul places sexuality inside covenant faithfulness.
Marriage.
One husband.
One wife.
Mutual responsibility.
Mutual belonging.
Mutual faithfulness.
And immediately after verse 2, Paul becomes even more startlingly practical.
The husband is to give his wife the marital affection and intimacy due to her, and the wife likewise to her husband.
Then Paul describes an extraordinary mutuality: the husband does not treat his body as though his wife does not matter, and the wife does not treat hers as though her husband does not matter.
In a world where sexual relationships could easily become about male appetite, domination, exploitation, and entitlement, Paul addresses both husband and wife.
“Each man…”
“Each woman…”
“The husband…”
“The wife…”
Again and again, reciprocity.
Christian marital intimacy is not supposed to be one person using another person.
It is covenantal self-giving.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because someone could read “because of sexual immorality” and come away with the crude idea:
So Paul is basically saying, “If you're sexually tempted, get married so you can have sex.”
No.
That is far too shallow.
Marriage is not God's loophole for lust.
A wedding ring does not sanctify selfishness.
A marriage certificate does not turn another human being into an instrument for satisfying your appetites.
And your spouse is not God's approved substitute for pornography.
Marriage is covenant.
Marriage asks something lust hates to give:
faithfulness.
Lust says, “I want your body.”
Covenant says, “I give you myself.”
Lust consumes.
Love serves.
Lust asks, “What can I get?”
Christlike love asks, “What can I give?”
Lust can survive without knowing someone's soul.
Marriage calls two people into a shared life of fidelity, sacrifice, forgiveness, responsibility, tenderness, patience, and perseverance.
This is why Paul's words become even clearer when we keep reading.

In 1 Corinthians 7:5, he warns married couples not to deprive one another except temporarily by mutual agreement for prayer, after which they should come together again so that Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control.
Paul is realistic.
Temptation exists.
Bodies exist.
Desire exists.
Weakness exists.
Satan exploits weakness.
And marriage provides a God-ordained context in which sexual desire can be expressed faithfully rather than promiscuously.
But then Paul destroys another misunderstanding.
He does not command every Christian to marry.
In fact, immediately afterward he speaks positively about singleness.
Paul himself lived unmarried and wished others could share his gift, while recognizing that God gives different gifts to different people.
Then comes 1 Corinthians 7:9:
“εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν.”
Ei de ouk enkrateuontai, gamēsatōsan.
“But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry.”
Then:
“κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι.”
Kreitton gar estin gamēsai ē pyrousthai.
“For it is better to marry than to burn.”
The point is not that unmarried Christians are incomplete.
Jesus Himself destroys that idea.
The most complete human life ever lived was lived by an unmarried man.
Jesus Christ.
So marriage cannot be necessary for human completeness.
Christ is.
And this is where the passage becomes intensely personal.
Because maybe your deepest problem is not that you need a spouse.
Maybe you have been telling yourself:
“If I could just get married, this temptation would disappear.”
But marriage does not crucify lust.

Jesus does not promise that a wedding ceremony will suddenly erase years of pornography, fantasy, objectification, emotional dependency, secret messaging, masturbation, infidelity of heart, or patterns of using other people mentally for sexual gratification.
You can bring an undisciplined heart into a marriage.
You can bring pornography into a marriage.
You can bring fantasies into a marriage.
You can bring selfishness into a marriage.
You can even lie beside the person you promised yourself to while your imagination belongs to someone else.
Marriage can provide a holy context for sexual intimacy.
But marriage is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this desperately needed.
Because you have been waiting for circumstances to save you from something only Christ can transform.
“If I find someone…”
“If I get married…”
“If my spouse becomes more affectionate…”
“If my loneliness disappears…”
“If my hormones calm down…”
“If temptation stops…”
Then I will finally become holy.
But biblical holiness does not begin when temptation disappears.
Holiness is learning whom you belong to while temptation is still speaking.
Paul had already written:
“Ye are not your own.”
And then:
“Ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
The Gospel underneath Christian sexual ethics.
You were bought.
Not with silver.
Not with gold.
Not with religious performance.
Not because you finally conquered every sexual temptation.
You were purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
The hands pierced on Calvary purchased the hands you keep reaching toward temptation with.
The blood poured from His body purchased the body you have sometimes used against His will.
The eyes that looked upon sinners with compassion purchased the eyes you have sometimes allowed to wander.
And Jesus does not expose your sexual sin because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes darkness because He intends to bring His children into light.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God. Look what you did.”
The Gospel says:
“Run to Christ. Look what He did.”
Maybe you failed.
Maybe badly.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe there are browser histories nobody has seen.
Messages nobody knows about.
A relationship you know you need to end.
Pornography you promised God you would stop watching.
An affair of the heart that has never become physical—but you know what you have been nurturing.
Maybe your marriage looks respectable in public while becoming painfully cold in private.
Maybe your spouse feels rejected and you have stopped talking about it.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from being told either that your desires do not matter or that satisfying them is the only way to be authentic.
Scripture offers something deeper than either lie.
Your desires matter.
But they are not your master.
Your body matters.
But it is not your god.
Sex matters.
But it cannot save you.
Marriage matters.
But it cannot complete what only Christ can complete.
And temptation may be powerful.
But temptation is not lord.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Paul's answer to Corinth was not sexual shame.
It was sexual discipleship.
For some believers, that discipleship includes faithful marriage.
For others, faithful singleness.
For every believer, it includes belonging to Jesus.
That means the Christian question is no longer merely:
“What am I allowed to do?”
The deeper question becomes:
“How can I glorify Christ with the body He redeemed?”
That question follows you into dating.
Into engagement.
Into marriage.
Into singleness.
Into loneliness.
Into the hotel room.
Into the business trip.
Into the late-night scroll.
Into the private message.
Into the moment when nobody would ever know.
Except Him.
And perhaps that sounds frightening until you remember who “Him” is.
The One who spoke with the woman caught in adultery.
The One who welcomed sexual sinners others despised.
The One who knew everything about the Samaritan woman's tangled relational history and still offered her living water.
The One who went to a cross surrounded by sinners.
The One whose blood is sufficient for sexual sinners too.
Jesus does not minimize sin.
He paid for it.
That is infinitely better.
Grace is not Jesus looking at your chains and calling them freedom.
Grace is Jesus breaking the chains and calling you to follow Him.
So if you are reading this after falling again, do not turn this article into another five minutes of religious guilt before returning to the same darkness.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
If appropriate, seek mature Christian accountability.
Remove access to what repeatedly feeds your temptation.
Stop protecting the doorway through which destruction keeps entering.
If another person is involved in an immoral relationship, stop calling disobedience “complicated” merely because obedience will hurt.
If you have sinned against your spouse, pursue truth, repentance, wisdom, and restoration rather than simply becoming better at hiding.

If your marriage is struggling sexually, do not weaponize 1 Corinthians 7 against your husband or wife. Paul's teaching about marital intimacy is mutual; it is not permission for coercion, manipulation, intimidation, or abuse.
And if you are single, do not believe the lie that your life is on hold until somebody marries you.
Jesus is not a waiting room.
You can know Him now.
Serve Him now.
Become holy now.
Love people now.
Build His kingdom now.
Live fully now.
And if God eventually leads you into marriage, do not enter it asking another sinner to become your savior.
Enter knowing you already have One.
Maybe this article exposed something.
Good.
Not because exposure feels good.
It usually doesn't.
But wounds cannot be treated while we keep pretending they aren't there.
So be honest.
Not performatively religious.
Not polished.
Honest.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting.
Someone may choose confession instead of another night of secrecy because you were brave enough to say four words.
Someone may remember that struggling is not the same thing as surrendering.
And someone desperately needs to hear what you now know:
Sexual sin can become part of your story without becoming the final sentence of your story.
Because Jesus rewrites stories.
You may never know who.
The husband who looks happy in the family photographs.
The teenager who discovered pornography years before anyone realized it.
The Christian woman too ashamed to tell anyone what she is fighting.
The single believer convinced marriage will magically fix everything.
The wounded spouse wondering whether restoration is possible.
The person who believes sexual failure has permanently disqualified them from coming home to God.
If tagging them could embarrass them, send it privately instead.
Not because every sentence will feel urgent today.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support buys a blessing.
It doesn't.
Paul taught believers to give as they had purposed in their hearts, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Christian generosity is worship precisely because it comes freely from a heart responding to grace.
Your support becomes practical partnership.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you open your Bible again…
If something published here helped you repent…
If it helped you fight another day…
If it reminded you that Jesus had not abandoned you…
If these messages are reaching places where wounded people are hiding…
Then prayerfully consider helping keep them moving.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Point people toward Christ.
Because ultimately this is not about building an audience.
It is about reaching people.
Not collecting religious consumers.
Making disciples.
Not making sinners dependent upon a page.
Pointing sinners toward a Savior.
And perhaps tonight the sinner who most needs that Savior is you.
Then come.
You do not need to clean yourself before approaching the One whose blood cleans sinners.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come without excuses.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the body you misused.
Bring Him the heart you cannot repair.
Bring Him everything.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of good people proving they never became dirty.
It is the story of guilty people discovering that the blood of Jesus Christ is stronger than their stain.
Corinth had sexual sinners.
Jesus built a church there.
Corinth had broken histories.
Jesus washed people there.
Corinth had temptation.
Jesus called people holy there.
And whatever your history is, your darkest chapter does not possess the authority to write your final sentence.
Christ does.
So when temptation whispers, “This is who you are,” remember the cross.
When shame whispers, “Hide,” remember the empty tomb.
When lust whispers, “You need this,” remember the Savior who said that whoever comes to Him will never ultimately find Him insufficient.
And when your past whispers, “There is no coming back from this,” remember three words:
But ye are washed.
That is scandal becoming grace.
That is shame meeting blood.
That is captivity meeting Christ.
That is the sinner discovering that Jesus did not come merely to improve behavior.
He came to make dead people alive.

And one day, when every secret has lost its power, every temptation has finally fallen silent, and every redeemed body stands resurrected before its Redeemer, nobody will be boasting that they were strong enough to save themselves.
We will look at the Lamb.
The scars.
The blood.
The grace.
And we will know who brought us home.
Your sin may explain a chapter of your story—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
